warmup.text: Before you read, answer the question on the card in your reading journal. Then set your lens. This week is all about voice: the way Fleischman sounds like nobody else. Listen for it from the very first page.

words.text: This week's endings are o u s, which means full of, i v e, which means tending to, and i t y, which names a quality. The spelling focus is word families, words that grow from one base. In the game, every right word hauls the bucket up the coyote hole.

reading.text: Read Chapter 13, A Bushel of Neckties. The partners settle into the diggings, and then comes an auction. Watch what Jack does when one small word costs him real gold. Then try the Read Like a Writer box.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 13. Then plan your revision. Copy one paragraph from your adventure draft, and list three spots to change: one for voice, one for dialogue, and one for description.

glossary.meaning: the way a writer sounds on the page, like a speaking voice
an ending added to a word that changes its meaning or job

ous: Three letters: o, then two more.
ty: This word names a quality. The i is already there.

miss.signature: sign + ature: the sign family keeps its silent g.
miss.signal: sign + al: you can see sign inside it.
miss.decision: decide + ion: the d becomes s.
miss.decisive: decide + ive: the d becomes s again.

game.title: Climb Out of the Coyote Hole
game.sub: This week's word game · 8 notches today
game.look: A coyote hole is a deep shaft miners dug straight down to bedrock, where heavy gold settles. Each right answer hauls the bucket of pay dirt up one notch of the rope. A wrong answer lets loose dirt slide it back down one notch.

do: Read the clue.
Tap the word that fits.
Tap Haul it up for the next clue.
how.why: A suffix is spelled the same way every time, and a word family keeps its base. Knowing both keeps your spelling right.

game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for eight more notches.

rounds.why: courage keeps its e before -ous, so the g stays soft.
rounds.miss: Keep the whole base word courage, then add -ous.

rounds.clue: Tending to catch the eye (bright neckties)
rounds.why: attract + ive: two t's, then c, t.

rounds.miss: Watch the ous: one letter drops before -ity.

rounds.why: mystery changes y to i before -ous.
rounds.miss: The y in mystery changes before the ending.

rounds.clue: Which word is in the same family as camp?
rounds.why: camp + fire: a fire in camp.
rounds.miss: Look for the whole word camp inside.

rounds.clue: Which word is in the same family as miner?
rounds.why: A miner is someone who works a mine.
rounds.miss: minor sounds the same but is a different word.

rounds.clue: Which word is in the same family as reputation?
rounds.why: repute + ation: what people think of you.
rounds.miss: Look for the base rep-u-t inside.
The ending here is -ative, with an a.

cards.title: Real history: how miners dug for gold
cards.intro: Pitch-pine Billy is made up. The ways he digs for gold are real.

items.meaning: Where gold lay deep, miners dug narrow shafts straight down, often 20 to 40 feet, to reach bedrock, where heavy gold settles. Miners were lowered into them in buckets.

A rocker, or cradle, was a wooden box on rockers. Miners shoveled in dirt, poured in water and rocked it, and the gold caught on wooden bars at the bottom. It washed more dirt than a pan, and two or three men often worked one together.
A long tom was a wooden trough 10 to 20 feet long set in running water. Several men shoveled dirt in, and the gold caught on bars at the bottom. It washed more dirt than a rocker.

In San Francisco, gold dust was traded at about $16 an ounce, a price merchants agreed on. Out in the camps, miners often got much less for it. The prices in Chapter 13 are the novel's, but prices in the camps really were very high, because everything had to be hauled in.

cards.note: Sources: California State Parks; Journal of Sierra Nevada History and Biography; H. H. Bancroft, California Inter Pocula (1888).

cards.title: A note before you read: words from 1963
cards.intro: This book was written in 1963. One line in Chapter 13 uses an old name for some of the people at the auction. Here is what to know.

items.meaning: The auction crowd includes Kanakas from the Sandwich Islands. Sandwich Islands was the old English name for Hawaii. Outsiders used Kanaka as a label for Native Hawaiians and other Pacific Islanders, often in an unkind way.

Kānaka is the Hawaiian word for people. Native Hawaiians sailed to California on trading and whaling ships long before the Gold Rush, and in 1839 John Sutter brought a group of Hawaiian workers with him. Many Hawaiians mined gold in 1848 and 1849, and places such as Kanaka Creek and Kanaka Bar are named for them.
The auction crowd, with miners from France, Mexico, Chile, Germany, Hawaii and the eastern states, is true to life. The gold fields drew people from all over the world.

cards.note: Sources: historian Benjamin Madley, Journal of American History (2024); California place names in Sierra and Trinity counties.

virtue.name: integrity
virtue.title: Keeping your word, or not?
virtue.intro: This week's virtue is integrity: keeping your word and doing what you said you would, even when it costs you. Sort these everyday examples.

items.t: You promised to help a neighbor rake leaves. A friend invites you to the movies, and you rake the leaves anyway.
items.why: You do what you said, even though something more fun came up.

items.t: You said you'd return a book on Friday, but you keep it because no one reminds you.
items.why: Your word should not depend on someone checking.

items.t: You agreed to a trade, then found out your card was worth more. You trade anyway.
items.why: A deal is a promise, even when it turns out to cost you.

items.t: You tell your team you'll be at practice, then skip because it's raining.
items.why: A little rain is not a good reason to go back on your word.
